title: Vasquez elsewhere ranks believing oneself justified as a species of private faith
source_text: XLV. Sed quod mirum est ille ipse Vasquez, qui tam operose refutat Catharinum, certitudinem fidei divinae justis de sua gratia tribuentem, disputatione supra saepius allegata, alibi tamen ex professo docet, & probare contendit fidei nomen & rationem convenire illi persuasioni, qua quis credit se justificatum esse, quam vult esse quandam fidei speciem a Catholica, sive dogmatica distinctam. Nam fidei privatae, quae Catholicae opponitur, & quae non convenit omnibus, sed aliquibus tantum, cujusque objectum toti Ecclesiae ad credendum propositum non est, enumerans varias species, dicit ad eam pertinere fidem, qua aliquis credit se justificatum esse. Postquam enim primam in eo ordine collocavit fidem, qua aliquis credit ea quae sibi peculiariter revelata sunt; secundam vero fidem miraculorum subjungit, Tertia fides est huic similis, nempe, qua quis credit se a Deo consecuturum aliquid quod tamen sibi soli specialiter promissum non est, ut cum quis credit se habiturum auxilium congruum ad justificationem, & perseverantiam, se etiam aeternam salutem adepturum, quia sibi gratia Dei efficax non denegabitur. Hujus etiam generis est fides, qua quis credit se a Deo per orationem obtenturum id quod petit, vel spirituale, vel temporale ad spiritualia pertinens. Addamus etiam fidem qua quis credit se justificatum esse. Haec enim etiam ad donum Dei pertinet, si homo id credat sicut oportet. In 1.2. Tom. 2. Disp. 200. cap. 4.
pass_a_gloss: But what is marvelous is that Vasquez himself, who so laboriously refutes Catharinus attributing to the just certainty of divine faith concerning their grace, in the disputation often cited above, yet elsewhere expressly teaches and contends to prove that the name and reason of faith befits that persuasion by which someone believes himself to be justified, which he wants to be a certain species of faith distinct from the Catholic or dogmatic. For enumerating various species of private faith, which is opposed to the Catholic and which does not befit all but only some, and whose object is not proposed to the whole Church for believing, he says that there pertains to it the faith by which someone believes himself to be justified. For after he placed first in that order the faith by which someone believes those things which have been peculiarly revealed to him, and then subjoins second the faith of miracles, The third faith is similar to this, namely that by which someone believes he will obtain from God something which nevertheless has not been specially promised to him alone, as when someone believes he will have suitable help unto justification and perseverance, and that he will also obtain eternal salvation, because efficacious grace of God will not be denied him. Of this kind also is the faith by which someone believes he will obtain from God through prayer that which he asks, whether spiritual or temporal pertaining to spiritual things. Let us also add the faith by which someone believes himself to be justified. For this also pertains to the gift of God, if a person believes it as he ought. In 1.2. Tom. 2. Disp. 200. cap. 4.
pass_b_english: Vasquez’s anti-Catharinus zeal sits oddly beside his own ‘private faith’ taxonomy.
He lists believing oneself justified among non-catholic faith-species tied to God’s gift.
